title: Generating Permutations
summary: Generating every ordering of a set with backtracking, handling duplicate elements correctly, and the used-set vs. in-place-swap implementation trade-off.

slides.markdown:
A **permutation** is one specific ordering of a set of elements — `[1,2,3]` has six: every way of arranging three distinct items. Generating all of them is the [backtracking framework](backtracking-framework) applied directly: at each position, choose an element that hasn't been placed yet, recurse into the next position, then undo the choice before trying the next candidate.

This topic is where the general template meets its first real complication: **duplicate elements**. `[1,1,2]` doesn't have 6 permutations, it has 3 — and generating all 6 and de-duplicating after the fact wastes exactly the work backtracking is supposed to avoid. The right fix is pruning at the tree level, not filtering the output.

You'll also see two competing implementations — tracking used elements in a set, versus swapping elements in place — which trade memory for mutation complexity in a way that shows up again throughout this group.

Build a permutation left to right: at **position 0**, try every element as the first pick; for each choice, at **position 1**, try every *remaining* element; and so on until every position is filled, at which point the current path is one complete permutation.

This is exactly the choose/explore/unexplore template: **choose** an unused element for the current position, **explore** by recursing into the next position, **unexplore** by marking that element unused again before the loop tries the next candidate for this position. The recursion bottoms out — the base case — when the current path's length equals the input length; at that point there are no positions left to fill and the path itself is a complete answer.

The only new idea versus generic backtracking is *what counts as a candidate*: at each position, a candidate is any input element that hasn't already been placed earlier in the current path.

Track which input elements are already placed in the current path with a `used` boolean array or set, and skip any element already marked used:

```python
def permute(nums):
    result = []
    path = []
    used = [False] * len(nums)

    def backtrack():
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            result.append(path[:])
            return
        for i, num in enumerate(nums):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(num)
            backtrack()
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False

    backtrack()
    return result
```

The `path[:]` copy when recording a solution is essential — `result.append(path)` would append a *reference* to the same list object that keeps getting mutated afterward, so every recorded "solution" would end up looking like the final, fully-unwound empty path. This is O(n) extra space for `used`, on top of the O(n) path itself.

Instead of tracking used elements separately, swap the chosen element into the current position within the array itself, then swap it back after:

```python
def permute(nums):
    result = []

    def backtrack(start):
        if start == len(nums):
            result.append(nums[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            nums[start], nums[i] = nums[i], nums[start]   # choose
            backtrack(start + 1)                          # explore
            nums[start], nums[i] = nums[i], nums[start]   # unexplore (swap back)

    backtrack(0)
    return result
```

Elements before `start` are locked in as the path so far; elements from `start` onward are the remaining pool, and swapping candidate `i` into position `start` is the "choose" step — swapping back afterward is the "unexplore." No separate `used` structure is needed because the array itself encodes what's placed.

slides.subTitle: Extra space vs. mutating the input
slides.markdown:
| | Used-set | In-place swap |
|---|---|---|
| Extra space | O(n) for the used array/set | O(1) extra — reuses the input array |
| Mutates input | No — input array untouched | Yes — the input array is reordered during the search (restored by the final swap-back) |
| Order of output | Elements appear in original relative order at each choice point | Order at each level depends on swap positions, less intuitive to trace |
| Duplicate handling | Straightforward — sort first, skip a used-equal value at the same depth | Trickier — swapping can reorder duplicates, so the usual "skip if equal to previous" check doesn't directly apply |

Used-set is the more common default because it doesn't mutate caller-owned data and its duplicate-skipping logic (next slide) is simpler to get right. In-place swap wins when the array is already a scratch copy and the extra O(n) space genuinely matters, such as embedded or memory-constrained settings.

For `[1,1,2]`, treating both `1`s as distinct produces 6 permutations, but only 3 are actually distinct as sequences of values. The fix is **sort the input first**, then at each position, **skip a candidate if it equals the previous candidate at that same tree depth and the previous one hasn't been used yet** (in the used-set version).

Sorting first is what makes "same tree depth" mean "adjacent in the current candidate list" — without sorting, equal values could be scattered and the adjacency check wouldn't catch them. The condition "previous one hasn't been used" specifically means: at this position, if the identical value was already skipped over (not chosen) earlier in this same loop iteration, choosing it again here would just re-derive the same permutation the earlier branch already explored, so skip it.

The key insight: duplicates only need to be skipped **at the same recursion depth** — the same value can absolutely appear at every position across the final output, since the two `1`s in `[1,1,2]` occupy different positions in `[1,1,2]` and `[1,2,1]` and `[2,1,1]` — those are the 3 valid answers.

slides.sectionTitle: Skipping duplicates at the wrong level
slides.markdown:
A common mistake: skipping a duplicate value **anywhere it's already appeared in the path**, rather than only at the same tree depth within the current loop. That over-prunes and silently drops valid permutations.

For `[1,1,2]`, both `1,1,2` and `1,2,1` are valid, distinct permutations — each `1` is used exactly once, just in different relative positions. A check that says "skip this value if it's anywhere in the used path already" would incorrectly block the second `1` from ever being placed at position 1, because *a* `1` is already in the path — even though it's a *different* physical copy of the value that's still available.

The correct check is narrower and easy to misremember: skip a candidate only when it equals its immediate predecessor **in the current candidate list at this exact recursion call**, and that predecessor was itself skipped (not used) earlier in this same loop. That's a same-level, same-call check — not a check against the whole path built so far.

slides.sectionTitle: The permutation tree for three elements
slides.markdown:
For `[1,2,3]`, the root has three children — one per first choice. Each of those has two children — the two remaining elements for the second position. Each of those has exactly one child — the single remaining element for the third position. That's 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 leaves, one per permutation.

The branching factor **shrinks by one at each level** — this is the structural difference from subsets or combinations (covered in the next two topics), where the branching factor stays roughly constant or shrinks based on a target rather than "one fewer available slot." That shrinking branching factor is exactly why the total leaf count is n! rather than some other function of n.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the count is n!, and what that caps
slides.markdown:
At position 0 there are n choices; whichever is picked, position 1 has n − 1 remaining choices; position 2 has n − 2; and so on down to exactly 1 choice for the last position. Multiplying those together gives **n × (n−1) × (n−2) × ... × 1 = n!**, and generating all permutations is inherently at least O(n!) work, since that's how many outputs there are.

That growth rate is brutal in practice: 10! is about 3.6 million, entirely reasonable; 15! is over a trillion; 20! exceeds the number of atoms most systems could ever enumerate in a lifetime. This is the concrete reason "generate all permutations and check each one" is only ever viable for roughly n ≤ 10–12 in an interview setting — beyond that, the problem needs a fundamentally different approach (a greedy or combinatorial argument), not a faster implementation of the same brute-force generation.

slides.sectionTitle: Generating all vs. the next lexicographic permutation
slides.markdown:
"Generate every permutation" and "given one permutation, find the next one in sorted order" sound related but are solved by **completely different algorithms**.

| | Generate all permutations | Next lexicographic permutation |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | Every ordering, any order | The single next-larger ordering |
| Approach | Backtracking over positions | Scan from the right for the first descent, swap, then reverse the suffix |
| Time per call | N/A — produces all n! at once | O(n) to produce just the next one |
| Total work for all n! | O(n! × n) | O(n! × n) if called repeatedly, but each individual step is cheap |

The next-permutation algorithm never builds a search tree at all — it's a direct, in-place transformation on the array. Confusing the two is a real interview trap: "find the k-th permutation" or "find the next permutation" are asking for the second algorithm, and reaching for backtracking there means generating and sorting all n! candidates when a single O(n) pass would do.

Given n and k, "find the k-th permutation in lexicographic order" looks like it needs generating and sorting all n! permutations, but it has a **direct combinatorial shortcut** that skips generation entirely.

The key fact: fixing the first element, the remaining (n−1)! permutations of the rest are contiguous and equally sized in lexicographic order. So `k // (n-1)!` picks which remaining element goes first, `k % (n-1)!` becomes the new k for the remaining n−1 elements, and the process repeats — peeling off one correct digit at a time in O(n) total steps (with a sorted list of remaining candidates), no search tree at all.

Reaching for the backtracking generator here is the classic mistake: it's correct, but it's O(n!) work to answer a question that has an O(n²) (or O(n log n) with the right data structure) direct solution. Recognizing "this smells like it wants the k-th-permutation trick, not generation" is exactly the kind of pattern match interviewers are checking for.
